title: Quantinuum Chief Scientist Argues Physical Fidelity Trumps Gate Speed in Fault-Tolerant Scaling Race - Quantum Computing Report
gist: In the essay 'Fidelity First in the Quantum Race', Quantinuum Chief Scientist Harry Buhrman argues that physical fidelity, not nanosecond gate speed, determines practical time to solution. Higher fidelity cuts QEC overhead, while error mitigation can make superconducting chips up to 1,000x slower in effect. QCR counters that trapped ions remain orders of magnitude slower per gate, and that Quantinuum must speed up shuttling, cooling and decoding to make its Apollo system competitive by 2029.

insights.claim: Harry Buhrman argues that high physical fidelity, not nanosecond gate speed, is the main parameter governing practical time to solution, because raw gate speed without sub-threshold operation just produces computational faults faster.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Quantum hardware should be judged on fidelity-adjusted throughput, not headline gate speed.

insights.claim: Quantinuum reports physical gate fidelities of 99.9975% (one-qubit) and 99.921% (two-qubit) on its 98-qubit Helios. Its color codes show Λ = 12 error suppression per Δd = 2, reaching a 5.0 × 10^-6 logical failure rate per cycle at distance 7.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: These numbers support Quantinuum's claim to lead on the path to logical-qubit scaling.

themes.theme: QUOPS and the cost of error mitigation

insights.claim: The essay uses the QUOPS benchmark, which pairs computational reach (circuit volume executed reliably) with effective wall-clock speed. Quantinuum claims better reach than Google Willow and IBM Boston.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Vendors are promoting their own composite benchmarks, so compare these claims with care.

insights.claim: Buhrman argues superconducting systems lead on operations per second for small, localized circuits. Scaling them to utility-scale algorithms, however, requires error mitigation that multiplies sampling runs, making effective execution thousands of times slower (up to 1,000x by the cited metric).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: If this holds, superconducting speed advantages may disappear on utility-scale workloads.

insights.claim: Gate times in shuttled trapped-ion lattices, typically tens to hundreds of microseconds, remain orders of magnitude slower than nanosecond superconducting circuits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Wall-clock speed is still the trapped-ion weak spot that competitors will target.

insights.claim: For its planned fault-tolerant Apollo system to be commercially competitive by 2029, Quantinuum must speed up ion shuttling, laser-cooling cycles and real-time streaming syndrome decoding without vibrational heating that erodes physical fidelity.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Progress on shuttling and cooling speed is the key milestone to watch for Quantinuum's 2029 roadmap.
